notes: Set-wide: 21 stories for ages 6-12, drawn from the Pali suttas, the Vinaya, the Jataka, the Dhammapada and its commentary, the Nidanakatha (the life-story at the start of the Jataka commentary), plus one later telling (the swan) that is named as later. Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhists tell these stories differently; the text says 'many Buddhists' and never 'all Buddhists'.

Every Jataka lesson opens or is sourced with 'a Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives'. Jataka numbers follow Cowell's The Jataka (1895); please check each number (12, 33, 37, 57, 316, 407, plus no. 4 cited for Cula-Panthaka).

Gentlest telling throughout: the monkey king's death (no. 407), the quails' capture (no. 33), the deer going to the cook (no. 12), Devadatta's role with Nalagiri, Sona's bleeding feet and the crocodile's wish to eat the monkey's heart are left out or softened. Each choice is noted on its lesson.
Only one exact quotation: Dhammapada verse 5 from Max Muller's 1881 translation (day 20, English only; the Spanish paraphrases it). Please check the wording against SBE vol. 10.
Spanish uses 'el Buda', 'Siddhartha', 'la reina Maya', and keeps Pali names (Sakka, Rahula, Ananda, Nalagiri, Sona, Cula-Panthaka, Dona) unchanged.

Words of the day are a mix of Pali (Bodhi, metta, dana, anicca, Bodhisatta, Jataka) and plain English ideas (compassion, patience, balance). A Keeper may prefer Sanskrit forms (Bodhisattva, Dharma) in some places; day 21 gives Dharma with Dhamma alongside.

en.title: the baby born in the Lumbini garden
en.means: the full-moon festival when many Buddhists remember the Buddha

story.head: a queen on her way home
story.text: Long ago, Queen Maya was traveling to her parents' home to have her baby. On the way, she stopped to rest in a garden called Lumbini. The sal trees were covered in flowers, and the bees were humming.

story.head: a baby under the flowering tree
story.text: The queen reached up and held a branch of a sal tree. Standing there in the garden, she gave birth to a baby boy. The old story says two gentle streams of water, one cool and one warm, poured from the sky to wash them.

story.head: seven little steps
story.text: Then something wonderful happened, the story says. The baby stood up, took seven steps, and looked all around him, in every direction. Later tellings add that a lotus flower opened under each little foot.

story.head: lanterns on the full moon
story.text: The baby was named Siddhartha. He grew up to become the Buddha, the awakened one. At a festival called Vesak, many Buddhists light lanterns, bring flowers to the temple and remember him. In some places, on his birthday, children pour sweet tea or water over a small statue of the baby Buddha.

game.prompt: who or what? tap the pairs.
pairs: held a branch of a sal tree

en.breath: let's take four slow breaths. breathe in slowly, like a lotus opening under a tiny foot. breathe out slowly. one breath for each careful step.
en.carry: today I'll notice one lovely thing, like flowers in a garden.

grownups.source: The birth in the Lumbini garden is told in the Nidanakatha, the life-story at the start of the Jataka commentary. The seven steps and the streams of water appear in the Majjhima Nikaya (MN 123). The lotuses under his feet come from later tellings.
grownups.ask: how does our family celebrate when a new baby is born?

es.title: el bebé nacido en el jardín de Lumbini
es.means: la fiesta de luna llena en que muchos budistas recuerdan al Buda

story.head: una reina de camino a casa
story.text: Hace mucho tiempo, la reina Maya viajaba a la casa de sus padres para tener a su bebé. En el camino se detuvo a descansar en un jardín llamado Lumbini. Los árboles de sal estaban cubiertos de flores y las abejas zumbaban.

story.head: un bebé bajo el árbol en flor
story.text: La reina levantó el brazo y se sostuvo de una rama de un árbol de sal. Allí, de pie en el jardín, dio a luz a un niño. La antigua historia dice que dos chorros suaves de agua, uno fresco y otro tibio, cayeron del cielo para lavarlos.

story.head: siete pasitos
story.text: Entonces pasó algo maravilloso, dice la historia. El bebé se puso de pie, dio siete pasos y miró a su alrededor, en todas las direcciones. Relatos posteriores cuentan que una flor de loto se abrió bajo cada piecito.

story.head: faroles en la luna llena
story.text: Al bebé lo llamaron Siddhartha. Creció y llegó a ser el Buda, el que despertó. En una fiesta llamada Vesak, muchos budistas encienden faroles, llevan flores al templo y lo recuerdan. En algunos lugares, en su cumpleaños, los niños vierten té dulce o agua sobre una estatuita del Buda bebé.

game.prompt: ¿quién o qué? toca las parejas.
pairs: se sostuvo de una rama de sal

es.breath: hagamos cuatro respiraciones lentas. inhala despacio, como un loto que se abre bajo un piecito. exhala despacio. una respiración por cada paso con cuidado.
es.carry: hoy me fijaré en algo bonito, como las flores de un jardín.

grownups.source: El nacimiento en el jardín de Lumbini se cuenta en el Nidanakatha, la historia de vida al comienzo del comentario de los Jataka. Los siete pasos y los chorros de agua aparecen en el Majjhima Nikaya (MN 123). Los lotos bajo sus pies vienen de relatos posteriores.
grownups.ask: ¿cómo celebra nuestra familia cuando nace un bebé?

notes: MN 123 has the birth standing, the two streams of water (cool and warm), the seven steps and looking in all directions; it does not name Lumbini or the sal branch, which come from the Nidanakatha. The lotuses under each step are from later (largely Mahayana and popular) tellings; the text says 'later tellings'.
MN 123 also has the baby speaking ('I am the foremost in the world...'); left out for children. Keeper: is that omission acceptable?

Vesak: many Theravada Buddhists remember the birth, awakening and passing on one full moon; many East Asian Buddhists mark the birth on a separate day (e.g., Hanamatsuri, with sweet tea poured over the baby Buddha). The text keeps these separate ('in some places, on his birthday'). Please check this is fair to all three schools.
'Buddha' explained as 'the awakened one': standard gloss; no further etymology given.

en.title: Prince Siddhartha and the wounded swan
en.means: feeling for someone who is hurting, and wanting to help

story.head: swans over the palace garden
story.text: Young Prince Siddhartha was in the palace garden with his cousin Devadatta. High above them, a line of white swans flew across the blue sky. Devadatta had a bow and arrows, and he aimed at the swans.

story.head: a hurt swan falls
story.text: One arrow struck a swan, and it tumbled down into the garden, hurt and frightened. Siddhartha reached it first. He held it gently in his lap, drew out the arrow, and laid cool leaves and honey on the wound.

story.head: two cousins want one swan
story.text: Devadatta came looking for the bird. “That swan is mine,” he said. “My arrow brought it down.” Siddhartha held it close. “It is mine,” he said, “because I saved its life.” Neither cousin would give in.

story.head: the wise ones decide
story.text: So they asked the wise people of the court to decide. They said that the one who saves a life has more right to it than the one who tried to take it. The swan stayed with Siddhartha. In many tellings, he cared for it until it could fly free.

items: Devadatta's arrow struck a swan.
yes: the swan tumbled down into the palace garden, hurt.
Siddhartha wrapped the swan in a soft blanket.
not in it: he drew out the arrow and laid cool leaves and honey on the wound.
wise people decided the swan should stay with the one who saved it.
yes: saving a life gives more right than trying to take it.

en.breath: take four slow breaths, soft and gentle, like the prince holding the swan in his lap until it felt safe again.
en.carry: I can be gentle with every animal I meet today.

grownups.source: This is a later telling of the Buddha's childhood, not found in the oldest Pali texts. Edwin Arnold's poem The Light of Asia (1879) tells it, and it is often told to children. Tellings differ in small details.
grownups.ask: if we found a hurt animal, what could we do together to help it?

es.title: el príncipe Siddhartha y el cisne herido
es.means: sentir con alguien que sufre y querer ayudarlo

story.head: cisnes sobre el jardín del palacio
story.text: El joven príncipe Siddhartha estaba en el jardín del palacio con su primo Devadatta. Muy alto, una fila de cisnes blancos cruzaba el cielo azul. Devadatta tenía un arco y flechas, y apuntó a los cisnes.

story.head: cae un cisne herido
story.text: Una flecha alcanzó a un cisne, y el ave cayó al jardín, herida y asustada. Siddhartha llegó primero. Lo sostuvo con cuidado en su regazo, le sacó la flecha y le puso hojas frescas y miel sobre la herida.

story.head: dos primos quieren un cisne
story.text: Devadatta vino a buscar el ave. “Ese cisne es mío”, dijo. “Mi flecha lo bajó.” Siddhartha lo abrazó. “Es mío”, dijo, “porque le salvé la vida.” Ninguno de los dos primos quería ceder.

story.head: los sabios deciden
story.text: Así que pidieron a los sabios de la corte que decidieran. Ellos dijeron que quien salva una vida tiene más derecho a ella que quien intentó quitarla. El cisne se quedó con Siddhartha. En muchos relatos, lo cuidó hasta que pudo volar libre.

items: la flecha de Devadatta alcanzó a un cisne.
sí: el cisne cayó al jardín del palacio, herido.
Siddhartha envolvió al cisne en una manta suave.
no está: le sacó la flecha y le puso hojas frescas y miel en la herida.
los sabios decidieron que el cisne se quedara con quien lo salvó.
sí: salvar una vida da más derecho que intentar quitarla.

es.breath: haz cuatro respiraciones lentas, suaves y tranquilas, como el príncipe que sostenía al cisne en su regazo hasta que se sintió seguro.
es.carry: hoy puedo ser amable con cada animal que encuentre.

grownups.source: Este es un relato posterior de la infancia del Buda, que no está en los textos pali más antiguos. El poema de Edwin Arnold La luz de Asia (1879) lo cuenta, y se cuenta mucho a los niños. Los relatos varían en detalles.
grownups.ask: si encontráramos un animal herido, ¿qué podríamos hacer juntos para ayudarlo?

sources.work: The Light of Asia, Edwin Arnold (1879)

notes: A later telling: not in the Pali canon. Arnold's Light of Asia (1879) is the best-known English source; it also appears in some older Sanskrit/Chinese life-stories (e.g., the Abhinishkramana Sutra as translated by Beal, 1875). Keeper: please confirm which earlier sources you prefer to name.
Devadatta is a child here and is not called bad; his later role in the Buddha's life is not mentioned.
The swan being set free at the end varies between tellings; hedged as 'in many tellings'. Arnold's detail of cool leaves and honey is kept.
A child's shooting a bird is described plainly but without injury detail beyond 'hurt'.

en.title: Sujata's bowl of rice-milk
en.means: the path between too much and too little

story.head: a very thin traveler
story.text: Siddhartha left the palace to understand why people suffer and how they can be free. For a long time he ate almost nothing, hoping it would help him understand. He grew so thin and weak that he could hardly stand.

story.head: a gift under the banyan tree
story.text: He saw that going hungry was not the way. He sat down to rest beneath a big banyan tree. A young woman named Sujata came with a golden bowl full of rice cooked in sweet milk, and she offered it to him with joy.

story.head: strength comes back
story.text: Siddhartha took the bowl to the riverbank and ate the rice-milk. Slowly his strength came back. Not too much and not too little: many Buddhists call this in-between path the Middle Way.

story.head: a bowl floats upstream
story.text: When he had eaten, he set the golden bowl on the river. “If I am going to wake up,” he said, “let this bowl float upstream.” And the story says the little bowl floated up the river, against the current!

game.prompt: who or what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in and out slowly, four times. not too fast, not too slow, like the golden bowl drifting gently on the river.
en.carry: today I'll thank someone who makes food for me.

grownups.source: Sujata's gift and the floating bowl come from the Nidanakatha, the life-story at the start of the Jataka commentary. The early suttas say he gave up harsh fasting and ate again (Majjhima Nikaya 36). The Middle Way is named in the first teaching (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11).
grownups.ask: who makes food for you, and how could we thank them this week?

es.title: el tazón de arroz con leche de Sujata
es.means: el camino entre demasiado y muy poco

story.head: un viajero muy delgado
story.text: Siddhartha dejó el palacio para entender por qué la gente sufre y cómo puede ser libre. Durante mucho tiempo casi no comió, pensando que eso lo ayudaría a entender. Se puso tan delgado y débil que casi no podía mantenerse en pie.

story.head: un regalo bajo el baniano
story.text: Vio que pasar hambre no era el camino. Se sentó a descansar bajo un gran árbol baniano. Una joven llamada Sujata llegó con un tazón de oro lleno de arroz cocido en leche dulce, y se lo ofreció con alegría.

story.head: vuelven las fuerzas
story.text: Siddhartha llevó el tazón a la orilla del río y comió el arroz con leche. Poco a poco recuperó las fuerzas. Ni demasiado ni muy poco: muchos budistas llaman a este camino de en medio el Camino Medio.

story.head: un tazón río arriba
story.text: Cuando terminó, puso el tazón de oro sobre el río. “Si voy a despertar”, dijo, “que este tazón flote río arriba.” ¡Y la historia dice que el tazoncito flotó río arriba, contra la corriente!

game.prompt: ¿quién o qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala y exhala despacio, cuatro veces. ni muy rápido ni muy lento, como el tazón de oro que flota suavemente en el río.
es.carry: hoy le daré las gracias a quien me prepara la comida.

grownups.source: El regalo de Sujata y el tazón que flota vienen del Nidanakatha, la historia de vida al comienzo del comentario de los Jataka. Los suttas antiguos dicen que dejó el ayuno duro y volvió a comer (Majjhima Nikaya 36). El Camino Medio se nombra en la primera enseñanza (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11).
grownups.ask: ¿quién te prepara la comida, y cómo podríamos darle las gracias esta semana?

notes: In the Nidanakatha, Sujata thinks he is the spirit of the tree, to whom she had made a vow; left out for simplicity. The rice-milk in some tellings is shaped into 49 balls; left out.
'For a long time' used instead of 'six years' (tradition's number) to keep to the claims rule.
The words of the floating-bowl wish are paraphrased, not quoted from a translation.

en.title: the night under the Bodhi tree
en.means: awakening; the Bodhi tree is the tree where the Buddha woke up

story.head: a seat of soft grass
story.text: That evening, Siddhartha came to a great fig tree. A grass-cutter gave him bundles of soft grass, and he made a seat beneath the tree. He sat down and decided not to get up until he understood.

story.head: worries and wishes from Mara
story.text: In the story, a being named Mara came to make him give up. Mara sent wind and rain, worries and wishes, and said, “That seat is not yours!” Siddhartha stayed calm and still.

story.head: a hand touches the earth
story.text: “Who will say the seat is yours?” Mara asked. Siddhartha quietly reached down and touched the ground with his hand. The story says the earth itself answered for him, and Mara went away.

story.head: awake at dawn
story.text: All night he sat in peace, looking deeply at how things really are. As the dawn came, he woke up to the truth. From then on, people called him the Buddha, the awakened one.

items: Siddhartha sat on a seat of soft grass.
yes: a grass-cutter gave him the grass for his seat.
a lion lay down beside him to keep him company.
not in it: he sat beneath the tree, calm and still, all night.
Siddhartha touched the ground with his hand.
yes: the story says the earth itself answered for him.

en.breath: sit tall and still, like Siddhartha under the tree. take four slow breaths, and feel the ground holding you up.
en.carry: when I feel wobbly, I can touch the ground and breathe.

grownups.source: The awakening is told in the early Pali suttas (for example Majjhima Nikaya 26 and 36). The grass seat, Mara's challenge and the hand touching the earth come from the Nidanakatha, the life-story at the start of the Jataka commentary.
grownups.ask: what helps you feel calm and steady when you're worried?

es.title: la noche bajo el árbol Bodhi
es.means: despertar; el árbol Bodhi es donde el Buda despertó

story.head: un asiento de pasto suave
story.text: Esa tarde, Siddhartha llegó a una gran higuera. Un cortador de pasto le dio unos manojos de pasto suave, y él se hizo un asiento bajo el árbol. Se sentó y decidió no levantarse hasta entender.

story.head: las preocupaciones de Mara
story.text: En la historia, un ser llamado Mara vino para que se rindiera. Mara mandó viento y lluvia, preocupaciones y deseos, y le dijo: “¡Ese asiento no es tuyo!” Siddhartha se quedó tranquilo y quieto.

story.head: una mano toca la tierra
story.text: “¿Quién dirá que el asiento es tuyo?”, preguntó Mara. Siddhartha bajó la mano en silencio y tocó el suelo. La historia dice que la tierra misma respondió por él, y Mara se fue.

story.head: despierto al amanecer
story.text: Toda la noche se quedó sentado en paz, mirando a fondo cómo son las cosas de verdad. Al llegar el amanecer, despertó a la verdad. Desde entonces lo llamaron el Buda, el que despertó.

items: Siddhartha se sentó en un asiento de pasto suave.
sí: un cortador de pasto le dio el pasto para su asiento.
un león se acostó a su lado para acompañarlo.
no está: se quedó bajo el árbol, tranquilo y quieto, toda la noche.
Siddhartha tocó el suelo con la mano.
sí: la historia dice que la tierra misma respondió por él.

es.breath: siéntate derecho y quieto, como Siddhartha bajo el árbol. haz cuatro respiraciones lentas y siente cómo el suelo te sostiene.
es.carry: cuando me sienta inquieto, puedo tocar el suelo y respirar.

grownups.source: El despertar se cuenta en los suttas pali antiguos (por ejemplo, Majjhima Nikaya 26 y 36). El asiento de pasto, el desafío de Mara y la mano que toca la tierra vienen del Nidanakatha, la historia de vida al comienzo del comentario de los Jataka.
grownups.ask: ¿qué te ayuda a sentirte tranquilo y firme cuando estás preocupado?

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (the Avidure-nidana: the seat, Mara, the earth as witness)

notes: Mara's armies, weapons and daughters are left out; Mara appears only as wind, rain, worries and wishes. In Southeast Asian tellings the earth goddess wrings water from her hair; not included.
'At dawn' rather than 'when the morning star rose' (the morning star is in some Mahayana tellings). Keeper may prefer either.
The tree is a fig (the pipal, Ficus religiosa); called 'a great fig tree'.

en.title: the hare in the moon
en.means: the old tales of the Buddha's past lives

story.head: four friends in the forest
story.text: This is a Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives. Long ago, he was born as a hare. He lived in a forest with three friends: a monkey, a jackal and an otter. The hare taught them to be kind and to share.

story.head: a hungry traveler comes by
story.text: On a holy day, a tired, hungry traveler came by. The otter brought him fish. The jackal brought food he had found. The monkey brought sweet mangoes. But the hare ate only grass, and grass is no meal for a traveler.

story.head: the hare's great gift
story.text: “I have nothing to give but myself,” said the hare. “Please light a fire.” The hare shook his fur three times, so no tiny creature living there would be hurt, and leaped into the flames. But the fire felt as cool as snow!

story.head: a picture on the moon
story.text: The traveler was really Sakka, king of the gods, testing the hare's kindness. He lifted the hare out safely and drew his picture on the moon, so everyone would remember. On a full moon, many people say you can still see the hare.

game.prompt: who gave what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: look up at the sky, or picture the round full moon. breathe in slowly, breathe out slowly, four times, and imagine the gentle hare resting there.
en.carry: tonight I'll look for the hare in the moon.

grownups.source: A Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives: the Sasa Jataka (no. 316), in Cowell's The Jataka (1895). The traveler is Sakka, king of the gods.
grownups.ask: what is something small you could share with someone today?

es.title: la liebre en la luna
es.means: los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda

story.head: cuatro amigos en el bosque
story.text: Este es un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda. Hace mucho tiempo, nació como liebre. Vivía en un bosque con tres amigos: un mono, un chacal y una nutria. La liebre les enseñaba a ser amables y a compartir.

story.head: llega un viajero con hambre
story.text: Un día sagrado, llegó un viajero cansado y con hambre. La nutria le trajo pescado. El chacal le trajo comida que había encontrado. El mono le trajo mangos dulces. Pero la liebre solo comía pasto, y el pasto no es comida para un viajero.

story.head: el gran regalo de la liebre
story.text: “No tengo nada que dar más que a mí misma”, dijo la liebre. “Por favor, enciende un fuego.” La liebre se sacudió el pelo tres veces, para que ningún bichito que viviera allí saliera herido, y saltó a las llamas. ¡Pero el fuego se sentía fresco como la nieve!

story.head: un dibujo en la luna
story.text: El viajero era en realidad Sakka, rey de los dioses, que ponía a prueba la bondad de la liebre. La sacó sana y salva y dibujó su figura en la luna, para que todos la recordaran. En luna llena, mucha gente dice que aún se ve la liebre.

game.prompt: ¿quién dio qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: mira el cielo, o imagina la luna llena y redonda. inhala despacio, exhala despacio, cuatro veces, e imagina a la liebre tranquila descansando allí.
es.carry: esta noche buscaré la liebre en la luna.

grownups.source: Un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda: el Sasa Jataka (n.º 316), en The Jataka de Cowell (1895). El viajero es Sakka, rey de los dioses.
grownups.ask: ¿qué cosa pequeña podrías compartir hoy con alguien?

sources.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell (1895)

notes: Gentle telling: the fire is cool and the hare is lifted out safely; nothing burns. In the text the jackal's food (meat, a lizard and curds) was taken from a field-watcher's hut; softened to 'food he had found'.
In the text Sakka squeezes a mountain to make the 'paint' for the moon picture; left out.
A hare offering itself as food is the heart of the story; some families may find it intense. Keeper: is this the right telling for 6-year-olds?

en.title: the monkey king who made himself a bridge
en.means: one who is on the way to becoming a Buddha

story.head: a mango tree by the river
story.text: This is a Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives. Long ago, he was born as a monkey king. He led a big troop of monkeys who loved the sweet mangoes of a great tree beside the river Ganges.

story.head: the king's men surround the tree
story.text: One day a human king tasted one of those mangoes and loved it. He came with his men to find the tree. They saw the monkeys and surrounded it, planning to catch them in the morning. The monkeys were afraid.

story.head: a long bamboo cane
story.text: The monkey king leaped across the river. He tied one end of a long bamboo cane to a tree and the other end around his waist, and leaped back. But the cane was a little too short. So he held on to a branch and stretched his own body to make the bridge.

story.head: everyone crosses safely
story.text: One by one, the monkeys ran across his back to safety on the far side. The human king watched in wonder: this monkey cared more for his troop than for himself. He had the monkey king gently lifted down and looked after.

items: the monkeys loved the mangoes of a tree by the river.
yes: a great mango tree beside the river Ganges.
the monkey king built a boat for his troop.
not in it: he stretched his own body to make a bridge.
the human king watched the monkeys cross.
yes: he watched in wonder and had the monkey king gently lifted down.

en.breath: breathe in slowly and stretch tall, like the monkey bridge. breathe out slowly as each little monkey reaches the other side. four slow breaths.
en.carry: today I can help someone get where they need to go.

grownups.source: A Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives: the Mahakapi Jataka (no. 407), in Cowell's The Jataka (1895). In the full telling the monkey king is badly hurt and dies after teaching the human king about caring for his people; this telling ends before that.
grownups.ask: what does a good leader do for the people in their care?

es.title: el rey mono que se hizo puente
es.means: alguien que va en camino de llegar a ser un Buda

story.head: un mango junto al río
story.text: Este es un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda. Hace mucho tiempo, nació como rey de los monos. Guiaba a una gran tropa de monos que amaban los mangos dulces de un gran árbol junto al río Ganges.

story.head: los hombres del rey rodean el árbol
story.text: Un día, un rey humano probó uno de esos mangos y le encantó. Vino con sus hombres a buscar el árbol. Vieron a los monos y rodearon el árbol, pensando atraparlos en la mañana. Los monos tenían miedo.

story.head: una larga caña de bambú
story.text: El rey mono saltó al otro lado del río. Ató una punta de una larga caña de bambú a un árbol y la otra a su cintura, y saltó de regreso. Pero la caña era un poco corta. Así que se agarró de una rama y estiró su propio cuerpo para hacer el puente.

story.head: todos cruzan a salvo
story.text: Uno por uno, los monos corrieron sobre su espalda hasta la otra orilla, a salvo. El rey humano miraba asombrado: este mono se preocupaba más por su tropa que por sí mismo. Mandó que bajaran al rey mono con cuidado y que lo atendieran.

items: los monos amaban los mangos de un árbol junto al río.
sí: un gran mango junto al río Ganges.
el rey mono construyó un bote para su tropa.
no está: estiró su propio cuerpo para hacer un puente.
el rey humano vio cruzar a los monos.
sí: miraba asombrado y mandó bajar al rey mono con cuidado.

es.breath: inhala despacio y estírate, como el puente del mono. exhala despacio mientras cada monito llega al otro lado. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy puedo ayudar a alguien a llegar a donde necesita.

grownups.source: Un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda: el Mahakapi Jataka (n.º 407), en The Jataka de Cowell (1895). En el relato completo el rey mono queda muy herido y muere después de enseñar al rey humano a cuidar a su pueblo; este relato termina antes.
grownups.ask: ¿qué hace un buen líder por las personas a su cargo?

sources.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell (1895)

notes: Choice: the story ends with the troop safe and the monkey king lifted down and cared for. The monkey king's death, and Devadatta (as a monkey) jumping on his back, are left out of the children's text and named calmly only for grown-ups.
In the text the king's archers plan to shoot the monkeys at dawn; softened to 'catch them in the morning'.
Whether the cane was tied to his waist or his foot varies by translation; 'around his waist' used. Please check against Cowell.

en.title: kindness for all beings
en.means: loving-kindness: wishing every living being well

story.head: monks go to a quiet forest
story.text: Once, a group of monks went to a forest to sit and practice during the rainy season. Each monk chose a tree to sit beneath. But the spirits who lived in those trees felt crowded out of their homes.

story.head: strange sounds at night
story.text: So the tree spirits made strange sounds and smells to send the monks away. The monks could not settle down. They walked all the way back to the Buddha and asked him what to do.

story.head: like a mother with her child
story.text: The Buddha taught them a teaching about kindness. Just as a mother would protect her only child, he said, let your kind heart reach out to every living being: big or small, near or far, seen or unseen.

story.head: a friendly forest
story.text: The monks went back, wishing well to every creature as they walked. The tree spirits felt that kindness, and the forest grew peaceful and friendly. Many Buddhists still chant these words, called the Metta Sutta.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.
pairs: went to sit in the forest

en.breath: breathe in slowly. as you breathe out, send a kind wish: to someone near, someone far, a tiny bug, a big whale. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I'll wish three creatures well today: may you be happy.

grownups.source: The teaching is the Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sutta Nipata 1.8), paraphrased here; many Buddhists chant it. The story of the monks and the tree spirits comes from the old commentary on that sutta.
grownups.ask: who is someone far away we could send a kind wish to tonight?

es.title: bondad para todos los seres
es.means: bondad amorosa: desear el bien a todo ser vivo

story.head: unos monjes van a un bosque tranquilo
story.text: Una vez, un grupo de monjes fue a un bosque a sentarse y practicar durante la temporada de lluvias. Cada monje eligió un árbol para sentarse debajo. Pero los espíritus que vivían en esos árboles sintieron que les quitaban su casa.

story.head: ruidos extraños de noche
story.text: Entonces los espíritus de los árboles hicieron ruidos y olores extraños para que los monjes se fueran. Los monjes no podían calmarse. Caminaron de regreso hasta el Buda y le preguntaron qué hacer.

story.head: como una madre con su hijo
story.text: El Buda les dio una enseñanza sobre la bondad. Así como una madre protegería a su único hijo, dijo, deja que tu corazón bondadoso llegue a todo ser vivo: grande o pequeño, cerca o lejos, visto o no visto.

story.head: un bosque amigable
story.text: Los monjes regresaron, deseando el bien a cada criatura mientras caminaban. Los espíritus de los árboles sintieron esa bondad, y el bosque se volvió tranquilo y amigable. Muchos budistas todavía cantan estas palabras, llamadas el Metta Sutta.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio. al exhalar, envía un deseo bondadoso: a alguien cerca, a alguien lejos, a un bichito, a una gran ballena. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy le desearé el bien a tres criaturas: que seas feliz.

grownups.source: La enseñanza es el Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sutta Nipata 1.8), en paráfrasis; muchos budistas lo cantan. La historia de los monjes y los espíritus de los árboles viene del antiguo comentario de ese sutta.
grownups.ask: ¿a quién que esté lejos podríamos enviarle un deseo bondadoso esta noche?

notes: The sutta is paraphrased (the mother protecting her only child; beings big or small, near or far, seen or unseen). 'May you be happy' in the carry echoes the sutta's wish that all beings be happy; it is offered as a kind wish, not a prayer. Keeper: is that acceptable?
The commentary's frightening sights (ghostly forms) are reduced to 'strange sounds and smells'.

The sutta is called Metta Sutta or Karaniya Metta Sutta in different collections; it is part of the paritta chants in Theravada practice. 'Many Buddhists still chant these words' may be read as Theravada-centered; please check.

en.title: the partridge, the monkey and the elephant
en.means: treating someone as important and listening to them

story.head: three friends under a banyan
story.text: This is a Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives. Under a great banyan tree lived three friends: a partridge, a monkey and an elephant. But they didn't listen to each other very much.

story.head: the elephant remembers
story.text: “Let's find out which of us is the oldest,” they said, “and we will listen to that friend.” The elephant said, “When I was a baby, this tree was a little bush. Its top leaves tickled my tummy as I walked over it.”

story.head: the monkey remembers
story.text: The monkey said, “When I was a baby, I sat on the ground and nibbled the very top shoots of this tree. That's how small it was.”

story.head: a seed the partridge dropped
story.text: The partridge said, “Long ago, I ate a fruit from another tree and dropped its seed right here. This whole banyan grew from that seed!” So the partridge was the oldest. The monkey and the elephant honored him and listened to his good advice, and the three friends lived happily together.

items: the elephant said the tree once tickled his tummy.
yes: when he was a baby, the tree was a little bush.
the monkey said he planted the banyan seed.
not in it: the partridge dropped the seed; the monkey nibbled the top shoots.
the friends agreed to listen to the oldest.
yes: they honored the partridge and listened to his advice.

en.breath: picture a tiny seed growing into a giant banyan tree. breathe in slowly as it grows, breathe out slowly as it spreads its branches. four slow breaths.
en.carry: today I'll listen carefully to someone older than me.

grownups.source: A Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives: the Tittira Jataka (no. 37), in Cowell's The Jataka (1895). In the story the wise partridge is the Buddha in a past life.
grownups.ask: who is the oldest person you know, and what would you like to ask them?

es.title: la perdiz, el mono y el elefante
es.means: tratar a alguien como importante y escucharlo

story.head: tres amigos bajo un baniano
story.text: Este es un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda. Bajo un gran baniano vivían tres amigos: una perdiz, un mono y un elefante. Pero no se escuchaban mucho entre ellos.

story.head: el elefante recuerda
story.text: “Averigüemos quién de nosotros es el mayor”, dijeron, “y escucharemos a ese amigo.” El elefante dijo: “Cuando yo era bebé, este árbol era un arbusto. Sus hojitas de arriba me hacían cosquillas en la panza cuando pasaba por encima.”

story.head: el mono recuerda
story.text: El mono dijo: “Cuando yo era bebé, me sentaba en el suelo y mordisqueaba los brotes de arriba de este árbol. Así de pequeño era.”

story.head: una semilla que dejó la perdiz
story.text: La perdiz dijo: “Hace mucho, comí una fruta de otro árbol y dejé caer su semilla justo aquí. ¡Todo este baniano creció de esa semilla!” Así que la perdiz era la mayor. El mono y el elefante la honraron y escucharon sus buenos consejos, y los tres amigos vivieron felices.

items: el elefante dijo que el árbol le hacía cosquillas en la panza.
sí: cuando era bebé, el árbol era un arbusto.
el mono dijo que él plantó la semilla del baniano.
no está: la perdiz dejó caer la semilla; el mono mordisqueaba los brotes.
los amigos acordaron escuchar al mayor.
sí: honraron a la perdiz y escucharon sus consejos.

es.breath: imagina una semillita que crece hasta ser un baniano gigante. inhala despacio mientras crece, exhala despacio mientras abre sus ramas. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy escucharé con atención a alguien mayor que yo.

grownups.source: Un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda: el Tittira Jataka (n.º 37), en The Jataka de Cowell (1895). En la historia, la perdiz sabia es el Buda en una vida pasada.
grownups.ask: ¿quién es la persona más mayor que conoces, y qué te gustaría preguntarle?

sources.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell (1895)

notes: In the frame story the Buddha tells this when senior monks were not given lodging; the frame is left out.
Beat 3 is short by design (one memory). The partridge is masculine in English ('him') and feminine in Spanish (la perdiz), following each language's grammar.
The text has the friends living 'without respect'; softened to 'didn't listen to each other very much'.

en.title: the quails who lifted the net together
en.means: getting along, so everyone can work together

story.head: a bird-catcher's net
story.text: This is a Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives. Long ago, he was a wise quail who led a great flock. A bird-catcher kept throwing his net over the quails to catch them.

story.head: heads through the holes
story.text: The wise quail had a plan. “When the net falls,” he said, “each of us puts our head through a hole in it. Then we all fly up together at the same moment, carrying the net with us.”

story.head: up and away with the net
story.text: The next time the net came down, they did just that. Whoosh! The whole flock lifted the net high, flew to a thorny bush and dropped it there. Then they slipped out underneath, free and safe.

story.head: a quarrel on the ground
story.text: One day, one quail stepped on another quail's head by mistake. They began to argue: “You lift the net, then!” The wise quail saw that quarreling would make them weak. He flew to a new home with all the quails who wanted to stay friends.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, all together, like the quails rising with the net. breathe out slowly, like the net dropping onto the bush. four slow breaths.
en.carry: today I'll work with someone instead of arguing.

grownups.source: A Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives: the Sammodamana Jataka (no. 33), in Cowell's The Jataka (1895). In the full telling, the quails who keep quarreling are caught; this telling leaves that out.
grownups.ask: what is something our family can only do when we all work together?

es.title: las codornices que levantaron la red juntas
es.means: llevarse bien, para que todos puedan trabajar juntos

story.head: la red de un cazador de pájaros
story.text: Este es un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda. Hace mucho tiempo, era una codorniz sabia que guiaba a una gran bandada. Un cazador de pájaros lanzaba su red sobre las codornices para atraparlas.

story.head: cabezas por los agujeros
story.text: La codorniz sabia tenía un plan. “Cuando caiga la red”, dijo, “cada una mete la cabeza por un agujero. Luego volamos todas juntas al mismo tiempo, llevándonos la red.”

story.head: arriba y lejos con la red
story.text: La siguiente vez que cayó la red, hicieron justo eso. ¡Fiuuu! Toda la bandada levantó la red muy alto, voló hasta un arbusto de espinas y la dejó caer allí. Luego salieron por debajo, libres y a salvo.

story.head: una pelea en el suelo
story.text: Un día, una codorniz pisó sin querer la cabeza de otra. Empezaron a discutir: “¡Pues levanta tú la red!” La codorniz sabia vio que pelear las haría débiles. Voló a un nuevo hogar con todas las codornices que querían seguir siendo amigas.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio, todos juntos, como las codornices que suben con la red. exhala despacio, como la red que cae sobre el arbusto. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy trabajaré con alguien en vez de discutir.

grownups.source: Un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda: el Sammodamana Jataka (n.º 33), en The Jataka de Cowell (1895). En el relato completo, las codornices que siguen peleando son atrapadas; este relato lo deja fuera.
grownups.ask: ¿qué puede hacer nuestra familia solo cuando todos trabajamos juntos?

sources.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell (1895)

notes: Gentle ending: the capture of the quarreling quails is left out of the children's text and named only for grown-ups.
In the text the frame is a quarrel among the Buddha's relatives; left out.

en.title: the elephant and the people who couldn't see
en.means: how something looks from where you are

story.head: a king's curious idea
story.text: The Buddha once told this story. Long ago, a king asked for an elephant to be brought to his palace. Then he gathered some people who had been blind from birth, and he asked each of them to touch it.

story.head: each one touches one part
story.text: One touched the elephant's head. One touched an ear. Others felt a tusk, the trunk, a leg, the tail. “Now tell me,” said the king, “what is an elephant like?”

story.head: a pot, a basket, a post
story.text: The one who touched the head said, “An elephant is like a big pot!” The one who touched the ear said, “No, it's like a basket for sorting grain!” The one who felt a leg said, “It's like a post!”

story.head: everyone knows a little
story.text: They argued and argued, each one sure he was right. The Buddha said people can be like this: each knows one part and thinks it is the whole. Each of them was right about a little, and none of them had the whole elephant.

items: one person touched an ear and said it was like a basket.
yes: a basket for sorting grain.
one person climbed up and rode on the elephant's back.
not in it: each one only touched one part with their hands.
the Buddha was the one who told this story.
yes: he told it about people who each know one part and argue about the whole.

en.breath: breathe in slowly and notice one sound you can hear. breathe out. notice another. four slow breaths, four new things noticed.
en.carry: before I argue, I'll ask: what do you see?

grownups.source: The Buddha tells this parable in the Udana (6.4), an early collection of his sayings, about people who argue when each holds only one part of the truth. Paraphrased here.
grownups.ask: when did you and someone else see the same thing in different ways?

es.title: el elefante y las personas que no podían ver
es.means: cómo se ve algo desde donde tú estás

story.head: una idea curiosa de un rey
story.text: El Buda contó una vez esta historia. Hace mucho tiempo, un rey pidió que trajeran un elefante a su palacio. Luego reunió a unas personas que eran ciegas de nacimiento, y les pidió a cada una que lo tocara.

story.head: cada uno toca una parte
story.text: Uno tocó la cabeza del elefante. Otro tocó una oreja. Otros tocaron un colmillo, la trompa, una pata, la cola. “Ahora díganme”, dijo el rey, “¿cómo es un elefante?”

story.head: una olla, una canasta, un poste
story.text: El que tocó la cabeza dijo: “¡Un elefante es como una olla grande!” El que tocó la oreja dijo: “¡No, es como una canasta para limpiar el grano!” El que tocó una pata dijo: “¡Es como un poste!”

story.head: cada uno sabe un poco
story.text: Discutieron y discutieron, cada uno seguro de tener razón. El Buda dijo que la gente a veces es así: cada uno conoce una parte y cree que es el todo. Cada uno tenía un poco de razón, y ninguno tenía el elefante entero.

items: una persona tocó una oreja y dijo que era como una canasta.
sí: una canasta para limpiar el grano.
una persona se subió y montó en el lomo del elefante.
no está: cada uno solo tocó una parte con las manos.
el Buda fue quien contó esta historia.
sí: la contó sobre personas que conocen una parte y discuten sobre el todo.

es.breath: inhala despacio y fíjate en un sonido que puedas oír. exhala. fíjate en otro. cuatro respiraciones lentas, cuatro cosas nuevas.
es.carry: antes de discutir, preguntaré: ¿tú qué ves?

grownups.source: El Buda cuenta esta parábola en el Udana (6.4), una antigua colección de sus dichos, sobre personas que discuten cuando cada una tiene solo una parte de la verdad. En paráfrasis.
grownups.ask: ¿cuándo tú y otra persona vieron la misma cosa de maneras distintas?

notes: In the Udana the comparisons are: head, a pot; ear, a winnowing basket; tusk, a plowshare; trunk, a plow pole; body, a granary; foot, a post; back, a mortar; tail, a pestle; tail-tuft, a broom. Only head, ear and foot/leg are used. Please confirm.
In the text the men end up striking each other with their fists; softened to 'argued and argued'.
The title uses 'people who couldn't see' and the story says 'blind from birth' (as the text does). Keeper and an accessibility reader may want to check the framing is respectful.
In the Udana the parable is aimed at wandering teachers of other schools who quarrel; the children's text generalizes it to 'people'.

en.title: the Banyan Deer king
en.means: giving freely, without wanting anything back

story.head: two golden deer kings
story.text: This is a Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives. Long ago, he was born as a golden deer called the Banyan Deer. He led one herd, and another golden deer, the Branch Deer, led a second herd. Both herds lived in a king's park.

story.head: one deer each day
story.text: The king of that land loved to hunt, and his hunts frightened and hurt many deer. So the deer agreed that, instead, one deer each day would go to the king, and the rest could live in peace.

story.head: a mother deer's turn
story.text: One day it was the turn of a mother deer who was soon to have a baby. “Please,” she asked, “let me wait until my baby is born.” The Banyan Deer said gently, “I will go in your place.”

story.head: a king changes his heart
story.text: When the king saw the golden deer king come himself, he was amazed. He let the Banyan Deer and the mother deer go free. Moved by such kindness, he promised that all the deer, and the birds and fish and other animals too, would be safe.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.
pairs: asked to wait for her baby

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like a deer standing very still in a quiet park. breathe out slowly. four slow breaths, calm and brave.
en.carry: today I'll take a turn for someone who needs help.

grownups.source: A Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives: the Nigrodhamiga Jataka (no. 12), in Cowell's The Jataka (1895). In the full telling the deer go to the king's cook by lot; this telling stays gentle.
grownups.ask: how did it feel when someone did something hard to help you?

es.title: el rey Ciervo Baniano
es.means: dar con generosidad, sin esperar nada a cambio

story.head: dos reyes ciervos dorados
story.text: Este es un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda. Hace mucho tiempo, nació como un ciervo dorado llamado Ciervo Baniano. Guiaba una manada, y otro ciervo dorado, el Ciervo Rama, guiaba otra. Las dos manadas vivían en el parque de un rey.

story.head: un ciervo cada día
story.text: Al rey de esa tierra le encantaba cazar, y sus cacerías asustaban y lastimaban a muchos ciervos. Así que los ciervos acordaron que, en cambio, cada día un ciervo iría con el rey, y los demás podrían vivir en paz.

story.head: le toca a una mamá cierva
story.text: Un día le tocó a una cierva que pronto iba a tener un bebé. “Por favor”, pidió, “déjenme esperar hasta que nazca mi bebé.” El Ciervo Baniano le dijo con dulzura: “Yo iré en tu lugar.”

story.head: un rey cambia su corazón
story.text: Cuando el rey vio que el rey de los ciervos venía él mismo, se asombró. Dejó libres al Ciervo Baniano y a la mamá cierva. Conmovido por tanta bondad, prometió que todos los ciervos, y también las aves, los peces y los demás animales, estarían a salvo.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.
pairs: fue en lugar de la mamá

es.breath: inhala despacio, como un ciervo muy quieto en un parque tranquilo. exhala despacio. cuatro respiraciones lentas, tranquilas y valientes.
es.carry: hoy tomaré el turno de alguien que necesite ayuda.

grownups.source: Un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda: el Nigrodhamiga Jataka (n.º 12), en The Jataka de Cowell (1895). En el relato completo los ciervos van al cocinero del rey por sorteo; este relato es más suave.
grownups.ask: ¿cómo te sentiste cuando alguien hizo algo difícil para ayudarte?

sources.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell (1895)

notes: Gentle telling: the chopping block and the cook are left out of the children's text ('go to the king'); named only for grown-ups.
In the text the doe first asks her own leader, the Branch Deer, who refuses; that refusal is left out so no one is cast as unkind.
The text says the king grants safety to deer, then all four-footed creatures, birds and fish; summarized. Keeper: 'dana' as the word for self-giving here — or would you prefer 'compassion' (karuna)?

en.title: the gift the Buddha didn't take
en.means: staying calm and kind when things are hard

story.head: an angry visitor
story.text: One day a man came to the Buddha, very angry. Someone in his family had gone to live as a monk, and the man did not like it at all. He shouted many rude, unkind words at the Buddha.

story.head: a question about guests
story.text: The Buddha listened quietly. Then he asked, “When friends visit your house, do you offer them food?” “Yes,” said the man. “And if they don't take the food, whose is it then?”

story.head: it stays with the giver
story.text: “It's still mine,” said the man. “It is the same with your unkind words,” said the Buddha gently. “I don't accept them. So they stay with you.”

story.head: a quiet change of heart
story.text: The man was surprised. The Buddha had not shouted back or grown angry. The man grew quiet and thought about it. The old text says he later asked to become a monk and learn from the Buddha himself.

items: the man shouted unkind words at the Buddha.
yes: he was angry that someone in his family had become a monk.
the Buddha gave the man a bowl of food.
not in it: he only asked about food that guests don't take.
the Buddha said he didn't accept the unkind words.
yes: like food a guest won't take, they stayed with the giver.

en.breath: breathe in slowly. breathe out slowly, and picture an unkind word drifting away like a dish nobody takes. four slow breaths.
en.carry: if someone is unkind, I can stay calm and kind.

grownups.source: From the Akkosa Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 7.2), in the early Pali collection of the Buddha's talks, paraphrased here. The angry man is a brahmin of the Bharadvaja clan.
grownups.ask: what helps you stay calm when someone says something unkind?

es.title: el regalo que el Buda no aceptó
es.means: mantenerse tranquilo y amable cuando las cosas son difíciles

story.head: un visitante enojado
story.text: Un día un hombre vino a ver al Buda, muy enojado. Alguien de su familia se había ido a vivir como monje, y al hombre eso no le gustaba nada. Le gritó al Buda muchas palabras groseras y crueles.

story.head: una pregunta sobre los invitados
story.text: El Buda escuchó en silencio. Luego preguntó: “Cuando tus amigos te visitan, ¿les ofreces comida?” “Sí”, dijo el hombre. “¿Y si no aceptan la comida, de quién es entonces?”

story.head: se queda con quien la da
story.text: “Sigue siendo mía”, dijo el hombre. “Lo mismo pasa con tus palabras crueles”, dijo el Buda con suavidad. “Yo no las acepto. Así que se quedan contigo.”

story.head: un cambio tranquilo
story.text: El hombre se sorprendió. El Buda no le había gritado ni se había enojado. El hombre se quedó callado y lo pensó. El texto antiguo dice que después pidió hacerse monje y aprender del Buda mismo.

items: el hombre le gritó palabras crueles al Buda.
sí: estaba enojado porque alguien de su familia se hizo monje.
el Buda le dio al hombre un plato de comida.
no está: solo le preguntó por la comida que los invitados no aceptan.
el Buda dijo que no aceptaba las palabras crueles.
sí: como la comida que un invitado no acepta, se quedaron con quien las dio.

es.breath: inhala despacio. exhala despacio, e imagina una palabra cruel que se aleja como un plato que nadie toma. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: si alguien es cruel conmigo, puedo seguir tranquilo y amable.

grownups.source: Del Akkosa Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 7.2), en la antigua colección pali de las charlas del Buda, en paráfrasis. El hombre enojado es un brahmán del clan Bharadvaja.
grownups.ask: ¿qué te ayuda a mantener la calma cuando alguien te dice algo cruel?

notes: Dialogue is paraphrased, not quoted from Rhys Davids or another translation.
The text says the man went forth and became an arahant; the children's text says only that he asked to become a monk and learn.

en.title: the clever monkey and the crocodile
en.means: noticing what is happening, right now

story.head: a rock in the middle of the river
story.text: This is a Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives. He was born as a strong monkey who lived by a river. Each day he jumped to a rock in the middle, then to an island full of fruit, and back home in the evening.

story.head: a crocodile waits on the rock
story.text: A crocodile wanted to catch the monkey. One evening he lay flat on top of the rock, waiting. But the monkey stopped and looked. The rock seemed higher out of the water than usual.

story.head: hello, rock!
story.text: “Hello, rock!” called the monkey. No answer. “Rock, why don't you answer me today?” The crocodile thought rocks must talk, so he called back, “What do you want, monkey?” Now the monkey knew who was there.

story.head: a hop and a bounce home
story.text: The monkey said, “Open your mouth, and I'll come to you.” The story says that when a crocodile opens its mouth wide, its eyes close. So the monkey hopped onto his head and bounced to the bank. The crocodile said, “Monkey, you are wise and brave!”

game.prompt: who or what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, and notice what is around you, like the monkey noticing the rock. breathe out slowly. four slow breaths.
en.carry: today I'll notice one thing that's different from yesterday.

grownups.source: A Jataka story, one of the old tales of the Buddha's past lives: the Vanarinda Jataka (no. 57), in Cowell's The Jataka (1895). Other Jatakas tell a different monkey-and-crocodile tale, where the monkey says his heart is hanging in a fig tree.
grownups.ask: what did the monkey notice that kept him safe?

es.title: el mono listo y el cocodrilo
es.means: darte cuenta de lo que pasa, ahora mismo

story.head: una roca en medio del río
story.text: Este es un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda. Nació como un mono fuerte que vivía junto a un río. Cada día saltaba a una roca en medio del río, luego a una isla llena de fruta, y volvía a casa por la tarde.

story.head: un cocodrilo espera en la roca
story.text: Un cocodrilo quería atrapar al mono. Una tarde se acostó plano sobre la roca, esperando. Pero el mono se detuvo y miró. La roca parecía más alta fuera del agua que de costumbre.

story.head: ¡hola, roca!
story.text: “¡Hola, roca!”, gritó el mono. Nada. “Roca, ¿por qué no me contestas hoy?” El cocodrilo pensó que las rocas hablaban, así que respondió: “¿Qué quieres, mono?” Ahora el mono sabía quién estaba allí.

story.head: un salto y un brinco a casa
story.text: El mono dijo: “Abre la boca y voy hacia ti.” La historia dice que cuando un cocodrilo abre bien la boca, cierra los ojos. Así que el mono saltó sobre su cabeza y brincó a la orilla. El cocodrilo dijo: “¡Mono, eres sabio y valiente!”

game.prompt: ¿quién o qué? toca las parejas.
pairs: vio que la roca estaba más alta

es.breath: inhala despacio y fíjate en lo que hay a tu alrededor, como el mono que miró la roca. exhala despacio. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy me fijaré en algo distinto de ayer.

grownups.source: Un cuento Jataka, uno de los antiguos relatos de las vidas pasadas del Buda: el Vanarinda Jataka (n.º 57), en The Jataka de Cowell (1895). Otros Jataka cuentan otra historia de un mono y un cocodrilo, en la que el mono dice que su corazón cuelga de una higuera.
grownups.ask: ¿qué notó el mono que lo mantuvo a salvo?

sources.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell (1895)

notes: In the text the crocodile's mate longs to eat the monkey's heart, and the crocodile says so; softened to 'wanted to catch the monkey'.
The crocodile's closing words praise the monkey's qualities (in Cowell, a verse naming truth, wisdom, resolution and generosity or similar); simplified to 'wise and brave'. Please check.
The heart-in-the-fig-tree tale is the Sumsumara Jataka (believed no. 208) and also in the Panchatantra; it is named only generally in grownups.source because the number is not verified here.

en.title: Rahula and the mirror
en.means: to look back and think about what you did

story.head: an evening visit
story.text: Rahula was the Buddha's son. He had become a young novice, learning to live like a monk. One evening the Buddha came to visit him. Rahula got a seat ready and brought water to wash his father's feet.

story.head: a question about a mirror
story.text: After his feet were washed, the Buddha asked, “Rahula, what is a mirror for?” Rahula answered, “A mirror is for looking at yourself, to see how you are.”

story.head: look before, during and after
story.text: “That is how to look at what you do,” said the Buddha. “Before you do something, look: will it hurt me or anyone else? While you are doing it, look again. After you have done it, look once more.”

story.head: making it right
story.text: If something would hurt, the Buddha said, don't do it. If you see you did something hurtful, talk about it with a friend you trust, and try again more carefully. If it was good and kind, be glad, and keep on learning.

items: Rahula brought water to wash the Buddha's feet.
yes: he got a seat ready and brought water.
the Buddha gave Rahula a mirror to keep.
not in it: he asked Rahula what a mirror is for.
the Buddha said to look before, during and after.
yes: before you act, while you act, and after you act.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, and look inside, like looking into a calm, clear mirror. breathe out slowly. four slow breaths, still and clear.
en.carry: before I do something, I'll stop and look first.

grownups.source: From the Ambalatthika-Rahulovada Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 61), the Buddha's advice to his son Rahula, paraphrased here. The full talk also uses a little water left in a dipper to teach about honesty.
grownups.ask: what is one thing you did today that you're glad about?

es.title: Rahula y el espejo
es.means: mirar hacia atrás y pensar en lo que hiciste

story.head: una visita por la tarde
story.text: Rahula era el hijo del Buda. Se había hecho novicio, y aprendía a vivir como monje. Una tarde el Buda vino a visitarlo. Rahula preparó un asiento y trajo agua para lavar los pies de su padre.

story.head: una pregunta sobre un espejo
story.text: Después de lavarse los pies, el Buda preguntó: “Rahula, ¿para qué sirve un espejo?” Rahula respondió: “Un espejo sirve para mirarse a uno mismo, para ver cómo está.”

story.head: mirar antes, durante y después
story.text: “Así hay que mirar lo que haces”, dijo el Buda. “Antes de hacer algo, mira: ¿me hará daño a mí o a alguien más? Mientras lo haces, vuelve a mirar. Después de hacerlo, mira una vez más.”

story.head: arreglar las cosas
story.text: Si algo haría daño, dijo el Buda, no lo hagas. Si ves que hiciste algo que lastimó, háblalo con un amigo de confianza, e inténtalo otra vez con más cuidado. Si fue bueno y amable, alégrate, y sigue aprendiendo.

items: Rahula trajo agua para lavar los pies del Buda.
sí: preparó un asiento y trajo agua.
el Buda le regaló a Rahula un espejo.
no está: le preguntó a Rahula para qué sirve un espejo.
el Buda dijo que hay que mirar antes, durante y después.
sí: antes de actuar, mientras actúas y después de actuar.

es.breath: inhala despacio y mira hacia dentro, como en un espejo tranquilo y claro. exhala despacio. cuatro respiraciones lentas, quietas y claras.
es.carry: antes de hacer algo, me detendré a mirar primero.

grownups.source: Del Ambalatthika-Rahulovada Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 61), el consejo del Buda a su hijo Rahula, en paráfrasis. La charla completa también usa un poco de agua en un cucharón para enseñar sobre la honestidad.
grownups.ask: ¿qué hiciste hoy que te alegra?

notes: The commentary gives Rahula's age as seven; left out under the claims rule.
The opening teaching on lying (the water in the dipper) is left out of the children's text to avoid a guilt frame; named for grown-ups.
The sutta says to reveal a harmful act to the Teacher or wise companions; rendered 'talk about it with a friend you trust'. Keeper: is that fair to the text?

en.title: the wild elephant who grew calm
en.means: quiet and steady inside, even when things are wild

story.head: a wild elephant in the city
story.text: One morning, the Buddha was walking through the city of Rajagaha with his monks. Suddenly a huge elephant named Nalagiri came charging down the street. He had been let loose, and he was wild and angry.

story.head: people hurry inside
story.text: People shouted and hurried indoors. “Turn back!” they called to the Buddha. But the Buddha did not run. He stood still on the road, and he filled his heart with kindness toward the elephant.

story.head: a great trunk comes down
story.text: Nalagiri felt that kindness. He slowed down. He stopped. He lowered his great trunk and stood quietly in front of the Buddha. The Buddha reached out and gently stroked the elephant's forehead.

story.head: the gentle walk home
story.text: The Buddha spoke softly to him. The story says Nalagiri lifted dust from the Buddha's feet with his trunk and put it on his own head, to show respect. Then he walked calmly back to his stable.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, standing still like the Buddha on the road. breathe out slowly, and send kindness to something wild. four slow breaths.
en.carry: today I'll send a kind wish to someone who is upset.

grownups.source: Told in the Vinaya, the monks' rule books (Cullavagga 7), paraphrased. In that telling the Buddha's cousin Devadatta arranged for the elephant to be let loose; this telling leaves that out to keep it gentle.
grownups.ask: what helps you calm down when you feel wild inside?

es.title: el elefante salvaje que se calmó
es.means: estar tranquilo y firme por dentro, aunque todo esté agitado

story.head: un elefante salvaje en la ciudad
story.text: Una mañana, el Buda caminaba por la ciudad de Rajagaha con sus monjes. De pronto, un elefante enorme llamado Nalagiri vino corriendo por la calle. Lo habían soltado, y estaba salvaje y furioso.

story.head: la gente corre a sus casas
story.text: La gente gritaba y corría a meterse en sus casas. “¡Regresa!”, le gritaban al Buda. Pero el Buda no corrió. Se quedó quieto en el camino y llenó su corazón de bondad hacia el elefante.

story.head: baja una gran trompa
story.text: Nalagiri sintió esa bondad. Fue más despacio. Se detuvo. Bajó su gran trompa y se quedó quieto frente al Buda. El Buda extendió la mano y le acarició la frente al elefante con suavidad.

story.head: el regreso tranquilo
story.text: El Buda le habló con dulzura. La historia dice que Nalagiri tomó con la trompa polvo de los pies del Buda y se lo puso en la cabeza, en señal de respeto. Luego volvió tranquilo a su establo.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio, quieto como el Buda en el camino. exhala despacio y envía bondad a algo salvaje. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy enviaré un deseo bondadoso a alguien que esté molesto.

grownups.source: Se cuenta en el Vinaya, los libros de reglas de los monjes (Cullavagga 7), en paráfrasis. Allí, Devadatta, primo del Buda, hizo que soltaran al elefante; este relato lo deja fuera para que sea suave.
grownups.ask: ¿qué te ayuda a calmarte cuando te sientes salvaje por dentro?

notes: Believed to be Cullavagga VII.3; cited as Cullavagga 7 without the section number. Please confirm.
Devadatta's role (bribing the keepers) is left out of the children's text and named calmly for grown-ups; nobody is called bad.
Later tellings add a mother and baby in the elephant's path; not included.
In the text the elephant walks back backward, keeping the Buddha in sight; simplified to 'walked calmly back'.

en.title: Sona and the strings of the lute
en.means: not too much, not too little: just right

story.head: a monk who tried too hard
story.text: There once was a monk named Sona. He wanted to wake up so much that he practiced walking meditation day and night, pushing himself very hard. He grew tired and discouraged, and he thought about giving up.

story.head: a question about music
story.text: The Buddha came to see him. “Sona,” he asked, “before you became a monk, you played the lute, didn't you?” “Yes,” said Sona. He had been skilled at it.

story.head: too tight or too loose?
story.text: “When the strings are too tight, does the lute sound sweet?” “No,” said Sona. “And when they're too loose?” “No.” “And when they're not too tight and not too loose?” “Then it sounds just right.”

story.head: tuned just right
story.text: “Trying is like that,” the Buddha said. “Too hard, and you get restless. Too soft, and you get lazy. Find the balance in between.” Sona listened, practiced this way, and found the peace he was looking for.

items: Sona used to play the lute.
yes: he was skilled at it before he became a monk.
the Buddha gave Sona a new lute.
not in it: they only talked about how lute strings sound.
strings that are too tight don't sound sweet.
yes: not too tight and not too loose is just right.

en.breath: breathe in, not too fast, not too slow. breathe out the same way, like tuning a string just right. four slow breaths.
en.carry: today I'll try my best, and rest when I need to.

grownups.source: From the Sona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 6.55), paraphrased. The Vinaya (Mahavagga 5) tells the same meeting between the Buddha and Sona Kolivisa.
grownups.ask: when do you try too hard, and when could you try a little harder?

es.title: Sona y las cuerdas del laúd
es.means: ni demasiado ni muy poco: justo lo necesario

story.head: un monje que se esforzaba demasiado
story.text: Había una vez un monje llamado Sona. Quería despertar con tantas ganas que practicaba la meditación caminando día y noche, exigiéndose muchísimo. Se cansó y se desanimó, y pensó en rendirse.

story.head: una pregunta sobre la música
story.text: El Buda fue a verlo. “Sona”, le preguntó, “antes de ser monje tocabas el laúd, ¿verdad?” “Sí”, dijo Sona. Era muy hábil tocándolo.

story.head: ¿muy tensas o muy flojas?
story.text: “Cuando las cuerdas están muy tensas, ¿suena dulce el laúd?” “No”, dijo Sona. “¿Y cuando están muy flojas?” “No.” “¿Y cuando no están ni muy tensas ni muy flojas?” “Entonces suena justo bien.”

story.head: afinado justo bien
story.text: “Esforzarse es así”, dijo el Buda. “Demasiado, y te pones inquieto. Muy poco, y te da pereza. Encuentra el equilibrio en medio.” Sona escuchó, practicó así y encontró la paz que buscaba.

items: Sona tocaba el laúd.
sí: era hábil tocándolo antes de hacerse monje.
el Buda le regaló a Sona un laúd nuevo.
no está: solo hablaron de cómo suenan las cuerdas del laúd.
las cuerdas muy tensas no suenan dulce.
sí: ni muy tensas ni muy flojas es justo bien.

es.breath: inhala, ni muy rápido ni muy lento. exhala igual, como cuando afinas una cuerda justo bien. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy daré lo mejor de mí, y descansaré cuando lo necesite.

grownups.source: Del Sona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 6.55), en paráfrasis. El Vinaya (Mahavagga 5) cuenta el mismo encuentro entre el Buda y Sona Kolivisa.
grownups.ask: ¿cuándo te esfuerzas demasiado, y cuándo podrías esforzarte un poco más?

notes: In the text Sona's feet bleed from walking meditation; left out.
The instrument is the vina; 'lute' follows common English translations ('laúd' in Spanish). Keeper may prefer 'vina'.
The Vinaya parallel (Mahavagga V.1) is believed correct; please confirm.

en.title: the monk and the white cloth
en.means: change: nothing stays exactly the same

story.head: a monk who couldn't remember
story.text: Cula-Panthaka was a monk who tried and tried, but he could not remember even one short verse. His big brother, also a monk, thought he might never learn. Cula-Panthaka felt sad and was ready to give up.

story.head: a clean white cloth
story.text: The Buddha saw him and gave him a clean white cloth. “Sit in the sun,” the Buddha said, “and rub this cloth gently. As you rub, say: taking away the dirt, taking away the dirt.”

story.head: the cloth turns gray
story.text: Cula-Panthaka rubbed and rubbed. Slowly, the white cloth turned gray and grubby from his hands. He looked at it and thought: it was clean, and now it has changed. Everything changes.

story.head: a mind made clear
story.text: In that moment his mind became clear and bright, and he understood deeply. The monk who couldn't remember a verse became wise, and he went on to teach others. The story shows that everyone can learn, in their own way.

game.prompt: who or what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like the warm sun on the cloth. breathe out slowly, and let one worry go. four slow breaths, nice and easy.
en.carry: if learning feels hard, I'll keep going in my own way.

grownups.source: From the commentary on the Dhammapada (verse 25) and the opening of the Cullakasetthi Jataka (no. 4), old Buddhist story collections. Paraphrased here.
grownups.ask: what was hard for you to learn that you can do now?

es.title: el monje y el paño blanco
es.means: cambio: nada se queda exactamente igual

story.head: un monje que no podía recordar
story.text: Cula-Panthaka era un monje que lo intentaba una y otra vez, pero no lograba recordar ni un verso corto. Su hermano mayor, también monje, pensaba que quizá nunca aprendería. Cula-Panthaka estaba triste y quería rendirse.

story.head: un paño blanco y limpio
story.text: El Buda lo vio y le dio un paño blanco y limpio. “Siéntate al sol”, le dijo el Buda, “y frota este paño con suavidad. Mientras frotas, di: quitando el polvo, quitando el polvo.”

story.head: el paño se pone gris
story.text: Cula-Panthaka frotó y frotó. Poco a poco, el paño blanco se puso gris y sucio por sus manos. Lo miró y pensó: estaba limpio, y ahora cambió. Todo cambia.

story.head: una mente clara
story.text: En ese momento su mente se volvió clara y brillante, y entendió a fondo. El monje que no podía recordar un verso se volvió sabio, y llegó a enseñar a otros. La historia muestra que todos pueden aprender, a su manera.

game.prompt: ¿quién o qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como el sol tibio sobre el paño. exhala despacio y deja ir una preocupación. cuatro respiraciones lentas, suaves y tranquilas.
es.carry: si aprender es difícil, seguiré adelante a mi manera.

grownups.source: Del comentario del Dhammapada (verso 25) y del comienzo del Cullakasetthi Jataka (n.º 4), antiguas colecciones de historias budistas. En paráfrasis.
grownups.ask: ¿qué te costó aprender y ahora ya puedes hacer?

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary on verse 25 (the story of Cula-Panthaka)

sources.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell (1895)

notes: In the text his elder brother Maha-Panthaka sends him away from the monastery; softened to 'thought he might never learn' so the brother is not cast as unkind.
The phrase he repeats is rajoharanam, 'removal of dirt/dust'; rendered 'taking away the dirt'.

The commentary says he became an arahant and was later praised for skill in mind-made forms; simplified to 'became wise and went on to teach others'. Please check the Dhammapada verse (25) and Jataka number (4).

en.title: the footprints and the lotus
en.means: a water flower that rises and blooms clean above the pond

story.head: footprints with wheels
story.text: A man named Dona was walking along a road when he saw footprints in the dust. They were special: each one had the shape of a wheel in it. “Who made these?” he wondered, and he followed them.

story.head: a quiet man under a tree
story.text: The footprints led to the Buddha, sitting peacefully under a tree. Dona asked, “Are you a god?” “No,” said the Buddha. “A spirit of the sky? A spirit of the forest?” “No.” “Then are you a human being?” “No.”

story.head: a flower above the water
story.text: “Think of a lotus,” the Buddha said. “It begins down in the pond and grows up through the water. Then it rises above the water and blooms, and the water doesn't stick to it.”

story.head: remember me as awake
story.text: “In the same way, I grew up in the world, but the world doesn't stick to me,” he said. “Remember me as awake: as a Buddha.” Many Buddhists still use the lotus as a picture of a clear, kind heart.

items: Dona saw footprints with wheel shapes in them.
yes: so he followed them to the Buddha.
Dona brought the Buddha a lotus flower.
not in it: the Buddha only talked about a lotus, as a picture.
the Buddha said the water doesn't stick to the lotus.
yes: it rises above the water and blooms clean.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like a lotus rising up through the water. breathe out slowly as its petals open wide. four slow breaths.
en.carry: even on a muddy day, I can bloom a little.

grownups.source: From the Dona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 4.36), paraphrased. The lotus that rises clean above the water appears often in Buddhist art and teaching.
grownups.ask: what helps you stay kind even when things around you are messy?

es.title: las huellas y el loto
es.means: una flor de agua que sube y florece limpia sobre el estanque

story.head: huellas con ruedas
story.text: Un hombre llamado Dona iba por un camino cuando vio unas huellas en el polvo. Eran especiales: cada una tenía la forma de una rueda. “¿Quién hizo estas huellas?”, se preguntó, y las siguió.

story.head: un hombre tranquilo bajo un árbol
story.text: Las huellas llevaban al Buda, sentado en paz bajo un árbol. Dona preguntó: “¿Eres un dios?” “No”, dijo el Buda. “¿Un espíritu del cielo? ¿Un espíritu del bosque?” “No.” “¿Entonces eres un ser humano?” “No.”

story.head: una flor sobre el agua
story.text: “Piensa en un loto”, dijo el Buda. “Empieza en el fondo del estanque y crece a través del agua. Luego sube por encima del agua y florece, y el agua no se le pega.”

story.head: recuérdame como despierto
story.text: “De la misma manera, crecí en el mundo, pero el mundo no se me pega”, dijo. “Recuérdame como despierto: como un Buda.” Muchos budistas todavía usan el loto como imagen de un corazón claro y bondadoso.

items: Dona vio huellas con forma de rueda.
sí: por eso las siguió hasta el Buda.
Dona le llevó al Buda una flor de loto.
no está: el Buda solo habló de un loto, como imagen.
el Buda dijo que el agua no se le pega al loto.
sí: sube por encima del agua y florece limpio.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como un loto que sube a través del agua. exhala despacio mientras abre sus pétalos. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: aun en un día lodoso, puedo florecer un poquito.

grownups.source: Del Dona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 4.36), en paráfrasis. El loto que sube limpio sobre el agua aparece a menudo en el arte y la enseñanza budistas.
grownups.ask: ¿qué te ayuda a seguir siendo amable cuando todo a tu alrededor está desordenado?

notes: The sutta's categories are deva, gandhabba, yakkha and human; rendered 'a god', 'a spirit of the sky', 'a spirit of the forest', 'a human being'. The Buddha's 'no' to 'human' may puzzle children; the point (he has gone beyond these kinds of becoming) is carried by the lotus. Keeper: is this framing acceptable?
The sutta speaks of water, not mud; the children's text keeps to water and puts mud only in the carry ('a muddy day') as everyday imagery.
The footprints carry wheel marks (the text: thousand-spoked wheels); simplified to 'the shape of a wheel'.

en.title: the Buddha cares for a sick monk
en.means: looking after someone who needs help

story.head: a monk alone and unwell
story.text: One day the Buddha and his helper Ananda were walking past the huts where the monks lived. In one hut they found a monk who was very sick with a bad tummy. He was lying all alone, and his bed was dirty.

story.head: nobody was helping
story.text: “Why is nobody looking after you?” the Buddha asked. The monk said, “I can't do anything useful for the other monks, so they don't look after me.”

story.head: warm water and gentle hands
story.text: The Buddha asked Ananda to fetch water. Together they washed the monk gently. Then the Buddha held his head, Ananda held his feet, and they lifted him onto a clean bed.

story.head: look after each other
story.text: Then the Buddha gathered the monks. “You have no mother or father here to care for you,” he said, “so look after each other. Whoever would look after me should look after the sick.”

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like warm water poured with care. breathe out slowly. four slow breaths, and think of someone who might need a little help.
en.carry: today I'll check on someone who seems left out.

grownups.source: From the Vinaya, the monks' rule books (Mahavagga 8.26), paraphrased. The Buddha's words, that whoever would look after him should look after the sick, are paraphrased too.
grownups.ask: who do we know who might be lonely or unwell, and how could we help?

es.title: el Buda cuida a un monje enfermo
es.means: atender a alguien que necesita ayuda

story.head: un monje solo y enfermo
story.text: Un día el Buda y su ayudante Ananda pasaban junto a las chozas donde vivían los monjes. En una choza encontraron a un monje muy enfermo del estómago. Estaba acostado solito, y su cama estaba sucia.

story.head: nadie lo ayudaba
story.text: “¿Por qué nadie te cuida?”, preguntó el Buda. El monje dijo: “No puedo hacer nada útil por los otros monjes, así que ellos no me cuidan.”

story.head: agua tibia y manos suaves
story.text: El Buda le pidió a Ananda que trajera agua. Juntos lavaron al monje con suavidad. Luego el Buda le sostuvo la cabeza, Ananda los pies, y lo pasaron a una cama limpia.

story.head: cuídense unos a otros
story.text: Después el Buda reunió a los monjes. “Aquí no tienen madre ni padre que los cuide”, dijo, “así que cuídense unos a otros. Quien quiera cuidarme a mí, que cuide a los enfermos.”

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como agua tibia que se vierte con cuidado. exhala despacio. cuatro respiraciones lentas, y piensa en alguien que necesite un poco de ayuda.
es.carry: hoy buscaré a alguien que parezca quedarse solo.

grownups.source: Del Vinaya, los libros de reglas de los monjes (Mahavagga 8.26), en paráfrasis. Las palabras del Buda, que quien quiera cuidarlo a él cuide a los enfermos, también están en paráfrasis.
grownups.ask: ¿a quién conocemos que esté solo o enfermo, y cómo podríamos ayudar?

notes: The text says the monk had dysentery and lay in his own filth; softened to 'a bad tummy' and 'his bed was dirty'.
The text has the Buddha pour the water while Ananda washes; simplified to 'together they washed'.
The monks are not blamed in the children's text beyond 'nobody was helping'; please confirm the section number (Mahavagga VIII.26).

en.title: the elephant who looked after the Buddha
en.means: being kind and loyal to each other

story.head: monks who couldn't agree
story.text: Once, in the city of Kosambi, a group of monks began to quarrel. They argued and argued and would not make peace, even when the Buddha asked them to. So the Buddha went off quietly to stay alone in a forest.

story.head: a big elephant moves in
story.text: In that forest lived a great elephant who had also left his crowded herd. He found the Buddha and stayed near him. With his trunk he brought him water, and he kept the ground around him clear.

story.head: quiet days together
story.text: The two of them lived peacefully in the forest, the Buddha sitting in calm and the elephant watching over him. Back in the city, the monks thought again about their quarrel, and in the end they made peace.

story.head: an old rule about hatred
